result:
The world is saved every day at 3:12 in the morning and no one ever sees it happen.

That's when the man at the supermarket I used to live next to would wheel out the big gray bins and start restocking the yogurt. I couldn't sleep one summer and I would watch him from my second-floor window. Fluorescent light, humming coolers, the little squeak of his shoes. He didn't do anything dramatic. He took the old yogurts from the front, put the new ones in the back, wiped up a little spill that someone had left. He did this all night, aisle by aisle. By 6 a.m., the store looked like it had always been full. Like it had just happened on its own.

We love stories about creation. We don't have good stories about maintenance.

We have the Big Bang, the invention of the lightbulb, the founding of the company, the first kiss. We don't have festivals for the second year of a marriage, or the thousandth time you cleaned the kitchen. We think history is made by people who build things for the first time, but actually, history is held together by people who keep rebuilding the same thing over and over.

I think about this a lot.

There is a physics law that says everything wants to fall apart. Entropy. Leave a garden alone for a month and it becomes a wilderness. Leave a house alone for a year and paint peels and mice move in. Leave a friendship alone and it gets quiet and awkward. The natural state of the universe is not order. It's mess. It's dissolution. Order is the weird, temporary exception that requires constant energy.

That means maintenance is not low-skilled work. Maintenance is a war against the fundamental tendency of the universe.

My grandfather couldn't build anything to save his life. He tried to build a birdhouse once and it came out looking like a modern art piece about anxiety. But he could fix anything. He had this drawer in his garage - every grandfather has this drawer - full of random screws, little washers, bent nails he had straightened out and saved. He would sit at his workbench and take apart a toaster from 1978 and just stare at it for a long time, until it gave up its secret. He never read manuals. He believed that if you made something, you owed it a little respect to try to understand how it worked before you threw it away.

We live in a throwaway economy because we forgot that.

Consider libraries. I love libraries not because of the books - although the books are great - but because a library is one of the few places left where maintenance is visible. Someone has decided that these books, this knowledge, this quiet should remain available for free to anyone who walks in. So someone has to reshelve. Someone has to repair the spine when a kid drops a picture book in the bath. Someone has to update the computers and clean the bathrooms and tell the man sleeping in the reference section, gently, that he can't sleep there but he can stay all day if he reads. It would be cheaper and easier to close it. It would be more profitable to turn it into condos. The fact that it is still there at all is a quiet, daily act of civic stubbornness.

The same is true for a trail in the woods. The trail doesn't exist by itself. If no one walks it, it disappears in a season. Nettles over it, trees fall across it. Every trail you have ever loved was kept open by boots you never saw.

I once hiked a section of the Pacific Crest Trail for a week with a friend. We met a trail crew - four people, in their twenties, sunburned, filthy, carrying tools called Pulaskis that look like an axe mixed with a hoe. They were doing what they called "brushing." Cutting back the manzanita that tries to reclaim the trail every spring. We thanked them profusely, like they were heroes, and they looked embarrassed. One of them said, "If we don't do it, no one gets to walk here." That was the whole philosophy.

It struck me that most of the important jobs can be described that simply.

If we don't do it, no one gets to walk here.

I think the internet has made this harder to see. The internet looks like it maintains itself. You post a photo and it stays there forever, right? Except it doesn't. There's a data center in Iowa humming so loud the technicians have to wear ear protection. There's an undersea cable between Portugal and Brazil that a ship has to patrol. There's a moderation team reading the worst parts of humanity so you don't have to. There's an open-source maintainer in Ohio who hasn't slept properly in three years because a library he wrote for free for fun is now used by 20 million websites and everyone is yelling at him because of a bug.

Digital things decay, too. They just decay differently. They get bit rot, link rot, outdated dependencies. Someone has to keep patching.

The fantasy is that we will invent an AI or a robot or a system that will finally take care of maintenance for us, so we can just create forever. But maintenance is not a bug in the system. Maintenance *is* the system. Even if you have robots, someone has to maintain the robots.

Maybe that's why it feels so meaningful when someone takes care of something.

Think about the last time someone really maintained you. Not celebrated you, not praised you - maintained you. Made you soup when you were sick. Drove you to an appointment. Listened to the same story about your job for the eighth time without trying to fix it. Texted you first after a long silence. Those acts are not impressive on Instagram. They will never go viral. But they are the reason you are still functional.

We have inverted our values. We pay astronauts millions and we pay childcare workers minimum wage. We give awards for innovation and we give nothing for upkeep. But which one actually lets civilization continue?

So here's my proposal for a small rebellion: notice one maintenance worker this week and thank them. Not in a performative way. Not posting about it. Just notice.

Notice the janitor who cleans your office bathroom at night so you never have to think about where the trash goes. Notice the city bus driver doing the same loop for the tenth year in a row. Notice the lineman in the bucket truck fixing power after a storm. Notice your partner doing the dishes again.

And then, maybe, do a little maintenance yourself. Not because it will make you famous. Not because it will be finished. Because it will never be finished. Wash the same plate you washed yesterday. Pull the same weed that grew back. Write the same friend you drifted from. Tighten the same loose screw.

There is a Jewish concept called *Tikkun Olam* - to repair the world. It doesn't mean you will fix the world. It means you understand your job is to participate in its ongoing repair. You don't wait until you're powerful enough to do it all at once. You just pick up what's in front of you.

The world will still be broken tomorrow. The yogurt will still need restocking. The trail will still grow over. The kitchen will still get dirty.

And that's good news, in a strange way. Because it means you will always have a meaningful job to do. You don't have to invent something new. You don't have to be a genius.

You just have to come back at 3:12 a.m. and put things back where they belong.
